newsitem.title: USA: Aiming for the luxury crowd.
newsitem.headline: Aiming for the luxury crowd.

text.p: SAN FRANCISCO (Reuter) General Motors Corp. wants consumers to believe that its EV-1 electric car is made for everybody, not just the affluent. But for now, the rich are exactly the people GM wants to target to increase demand for its new pollution-fighting car.
"We need to reach a very upscale crowd for initial marketing of the EV-1," said David Verklin, managing director of Hal Riney & Associates.
Unfortunately, consumers most likely to buy the car first are also very hard to reach with television.
Verklin, whose San Francisco-based ad agency is overseeing GM's $10 million campaign for the car, said, "This crowd in general doesn't watch a lot of TV."

The agency decided that one place to hit them was last Sunday's Super Bowl, one of the few remaining events that cuts across the entire spectrum of viewers. GM got a 90-second television commercial for the EV-1 aired in Los Angeles during the Super Bowl XXXI broadcast for an estimated $200,000.
Verklin said the Super Bowl was ideal for reaching potential electric car buyers. "It's one of those very few events in television that just about everybody watches," he said.

But GM did not want to buy a $1.2 million national spot during the Super Bowl because the car maker is not ready for national mass market rollout. In fact, GM has already sold out of the few hundred EV-1 cars it initially created. The car can only be purchased through a leasing agreement which will cost the consumer $500 to 600 per month.

"Price is one big reason we are targeting so few markets right now," said Verklin. "Also, the car can only go about 90 miles on its current battery system without recharging. It just makes more sense right now for people who live in warmer climates who don't drive very far to invest in the EV-1."

GM launched the EV-1 campaign in late November with only 28 billboard ads -- three in San Diego, 24 in the Los Angeles area. The message, super-imposed over a bolt of lightning, was "You can't hear it coming, but it is."

The television campaign for the car followed soon after and featured the theme "The electric car is here." In the spot, hundreds of common appliances come to life, wrench themselves from their electric sockets, and gather out in the street to marvel at the new EV-1. The computer-animated spot has received nationwide attention and acclaim, although it only ran in Los Angeles, San Diego, Tucson and Phoenix.

"The spot has been so well-received," said David O'Hare, Hal Riney's creative director and creator of the commercial. "We ran the commercial in some Los Angeles movie theatres and people actually applauded."
The EV-1 commercial took about nine months to create, while the entire campaign took about two years, said O'Hare.
The four-market campaign is also supported by a number of print ads in newspapers and magazines. Marketing materials for the EV-1 can also be found at Saturn dealers in the target markets.

O'Hare also said that GM plans to stick with the efforts of the current campaign for an indefinite period of time. "GM wants people to get used to the idea of an electric car," he said. "We want to promote the EV-1 as a comfortable investment, not something high-tech and unattainable."
